topic: How does a crew spacecraft catch up with the International Space Station in under 8 hours?

news_hook.event: NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 (Crew Dragon 'Grace', Falcon 9) launched Oct 1 2026 at 11:10 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40, Cape Canaveral, and docked autonomously to the Harmony module's forward port at 7:05 p.m. EDT: 7 h 55 min launch-to-docking, called the fastest launch-to-docking of a U.S. spacecraft in ISS history.
news_hook.notes: Opened NASA's own station blog post (docking time 7:05 p.m. EDT, 7 h 55 min, 'fastest launch-to-docking of a U.S. spacecraft in the history of the International Space Station', crew names, hatch opening ~8:45 p.m.), the NASA launch-coverage release, the NASA launch release, the NASA liftoff blog, and ClickOrlando. IMPORTANT NUANCE: the claim is 'fastest by a U.S. spacecraft', NOT fastest ever. Russian Soyuz MS-17 (Oct 2020) did it in about 3 hours (two orbits), per NASASpaceflight (opened) and Progress did it before that. Say 'fastest American trip', never 'fastest ever'. The prior record (12 h 33 min, uncrewed Dragon CRS-31, Nov 2024) appears only in search-result snippets and in an Interesting Engineering article I opened; I did not open a NASA page stating it. NASA pre-launch pages said planned 7 h 50 min; actual 7 h 55 min. NASA pages disagree on port wording (pre-launch search snippet said 'space-facing'; NASA blog says 'forward port'); avoid specifying the port in the video. Space.com and SpaceX.com pages opened but returned no article text, so they are not cited as verified.

facts.claim: Crew-13 lifted off at 11:10 a.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct 1, 2026 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.
Dragon arrived and docked at 7:05 p.m. EDT, 7 hours 55 minutes after launch.
NASA calls this the fastest launch-to-docking of a U.S. spacecraft in the history of the space station.
Crew: NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins (commander) and Luke Delaney (pilot), CSA astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.
The spacecraft docked autonomously; crew and station crew monitor it.
NASA's pre-launch blog said Dragon would spend just under 8 hours in orbit phasing on the way to the station.
Julianna Scheiman (SpaceX/NASA Dragon program) said 'the space station was in an opportune spot in space' / 'we got lucky this time'; i.e. launch geometry was unusually favorable.
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (the 'opportune spot' quote only; the 'we got lucky' wording appears only in a search snippet, not in an opened page)

facts.claim: Previous US record was 12 h 33 min, set by uncrewed Dragon CRS-31 in Nov 2024.
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (secondary outlet, not NASA)

facts.claim: Typical Crew Dragon missions took 15 to 24 hours to reach the station.
Dragon Demo-2 (May 2020) approached the ISS about 19 hours after liftoff and soft-docked at 14:16 UTC May 31, hard capture ~11 minutes later.
Soyuz MS-17 (Oct 2020) caught the ISS in two orbits, about three hours, halving the previous six-hour (four-orbit) profile; before 2013 Soyuz took about two days / 34 orbits.
facts.value: ~3 h (2 orbits); 6 h (4 orbits); ~2 days (34 orbits)

facts.claim: After Soyuz reached orbit it sent its position and velocity to Moscow to confirm the insertion was good enough for the ultrafast rendezvous; a slightly off insertion or missed correction burn could cancel the fast profile.

ISS flies at about 400 km altitude (Wikipedia: 413 x 422 km perigee/apogee at time of page), at about 7.67 km/s (27,600 km/h), orbit period about 92.9 min, ~15.5 orbits/day, inclination 51.64 degrees.
NASA says the station orbits at 'five miles per second' (about 8 km/s, rounded), about every 90 minutes, 16 orbits per day, inclination 51.6 degrees.
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (NASA rounds; use Wikipedia/derived for 7.7 km/s and 92-93 min). Inclination also at https://www.nasa.gov/international-space-station-frequently-asked-questions/

facts.claim: In circular orbits, lower orbits have higher orbital velocity; higher orbits have lower velocity.
Firing thrusters to increase speed gives a different orbit with higher altitude (and decreasing speed gives lower altitude).
Rendezvous requires both spacecraft in the same orbital plane and the same phase (position along the orbit); launch windows are critical for plane alignment.

Dragon must launch when the station's orbital plane passes over the launch site, enter a slightly lower orbit to gradually catch up, and achieve precise phasing; where the ISS is along its path decides how soon pursuit can begin.
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (secondary outlet paraphrase, not a NASA statement)

facts.claim: Typical orbital-maneuver chain: launch to a selected orbit, burns to raise/lower/phase, navigation sensors measure position relative to ISS, staged approach with planned hold points and go/no-go decisions, soft capture, hard capture, pressure checks, hatch opening; final approach is only a few cm/s.
facts.value: hold points; few cm/s final approach
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (non-primary explainer; consistent with Demo-2 and NASA pages)

facts.claim: Crew-13 hatch opening was planned about 1 h 45 min after docking (about 8:45 p.m.).
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (planned time)

facts.claim: A phasing maneuver: a burn puts a spacecraft in a phasing orbit with a different period; the period difference over each orbit makes up the angle between chaser and target; the second burn returns to the original orbit at the target's location.
facts.value: period difference converts the phase angle into time
facts.how_verified: opened page and found this (note: that page's summary describes a speed-up into a larger orbit for a target that is ahead in the same orbit; for a chaser BEHIND the target the logic reverses, see f22)

facts.claim: Worked example: circular orbit speed v = sqrt(mu/r) and period T = 2 pi sqrt(r^3/mu). At 408 km altitude: 7.66 km/s, 92.7 min. At 308 km (100 km lower): 7.72 km/s, 90.7 min. The lower orbit finishes a lap about 122 s earlier, gaining about 7.9 degrees of arc per orbit on the ISS (about 950 km along the path).
facts.value: 7.66 vs 7.72 km/s; 92.7 vs 90.7 min; ~122 s / ~7.9 deg gained per lap
facts.how_verified: derived from Kepler's third law with mu=398600.4 km^3/s^2 and R_earth=6378.1 km, computed by me in Python; the 408 km choice is illustrative (not the actual Crew-13 altitude)

mechanism.title: Orbiting is falling sideways
mechanism.plain: The station is always falling toward Earth but moves sideways so fast, about 7.7 km/s, that the ground curves away beneath it. At about 400 km up, one lap takes roughly 92-93 minutes.
mechanism.why: Gravity is slightly weaker higher up, and the speed that exactly balances the fall at that height is about 7.7 km/s.
mechanism.visual_idea: Cannonball thrown harder and harder from a mountain until the arc misses the ground; then zoom to ISS with a 92-minute lap clock.

mechanism.title: You cannot just chase it
mechanism.plain: If you point at the station and fire your engine, you do not catch up: you speed up, and speeding up lifts you into a higher, slower path.
mechanism.why: Added speed carries you outward to a bigger orbit, and bigger orbits are slower per lap.
mechanism.visual_idea: Chaser behind the ISS on a ring; burn forward makes its ring bulge outward and the dot falls further behind.

mechanism.title: Drop lower to go faster
mechanism.plain: To gain on something ahead, you go to a slightly lower orbit, where the lap is shorter and you move faster, and you pull ahead of the station lap by lap.
mechanism.why: Lower circular orbits have higher speed and shorter period (about 7.72 km/s and 90.7 min at 308 km versus 7.66 km/s and 92.7 min at 408 km).
mechanism.visual_idea: Two concentric rings, inner dot lapping the outer one with a growing angle readout and a stopwatch showing lap times.

mechanism.title: Phasing: gain the gap
mechanism.plain: The gap between you and the station is an angle around Earth. Each lap in the lower orbit shrinks that angle by a few degrees, so you pick the lower orbit and the number of laps that close the gap exactly.
mechanism.why: The difference in period between the two orbits turns the angle into time: gap angle = laps x angle gained per lap.
mechanism.visual_idea: Wedge-shaped gap between chaser and ISS shrinking each lap; counter of degrees remaining.

mechanism.title: Launch at the right moment
mechanism.plain: The launch must happen when the station's path passes over the launch site, and when the station is the right distance ahead. This is why launch times are fixed to the second and why some days are luckier than others.
mechanism.why: You can only reach the station if you start in its orbital plane, and the fewer degrees you must close, the fewer laps you need.
mechanism.visual_idea: Spinning Earth under a tilted ISS ground track; launch site slides under the line; a green window appears.

mechanism.title: Fewer laps, earlier burns
mechanism.plain: The old Soyuz profile took about 2 days (34 orbits); later 6 hours (4 orbits) and then about 3 hours (2 orbits). Fast profiles compute the burns on the ground beforehand and need a very accurate launch; Crew-13 used about 8 hours of phasing.
mechanism.why: If the starting gap is small and the first burn comes soon after reaching orbit, you need fewer laps; the tradeoff is less slack, because a missed burn or off-target orbit cancels the fast plan.
mechanism.visual_idea: Three timelines (2 days, 6 h, 3 h) with burn markers; Crew-13 timeline at 7 h 55 min.

mechanism.title: Raise up and slow in
mechanism.plain: As the gap closes, thrusters raise the orbit back up to the station's height and the ship ends up a few kilometres behind and just below it, matching speed.
mechanism.why: A burn at the right point lifts the opposite side of your orbit so you stop gaining and settle into the station's orbit.
mechanism.visual_idea: Burn flash at a marked point, orbit ring expands to coincide with the ISS ring; relative-speed readout falls toward zero. (Mechanism taken from standard theory, no opened source states Crew-13's exact burn sequence.)

mechanism.title: Approach with checkpoints
mechanism.plain: Close in, sensors measure the station's position, and the ship stops at planned hold points where teams check for a go or no-go before moving on. Final approach is only a few centimetres per second.
mechanism.why: At tiny distances, a small error can mean a collision, so speed and checks matter more than speed itself.
mechanism.visual_idea: Ladder of checkpoint markers shrinking toward the port with GO/NO-GO flags (do not put distances on screen: not verified for Crew-13).

mechanism.title: Self-docking and latching
mechanism.plain: Dragon flies itself in. First a soft capture links the two vehicles, then hooks pull them rigid, and after leak checks the hatch opens. Crew-13: docked 7:05 p.m., hatch about 8:45 p.m.
mechanism.why: Computers react faster and more smoothly than a person at these tiny margins, and humans on both sides watch and can intervene.
mechanism.visual_idea: Close-up of the docking ring: soft capture, 12 hooks (Demo-2 detail) close, pressure gauge, hatch swings open.

counterintuitive_core: In orbit, going faster does not catch you up: it lifts you into a higher, slower orbit. To catch something ahead, you drop to a lower orbit where you move faster and your lap is shorter. You gain on it a few degrees each lap, then climb back up to meet it. (Chasing from behind. Sources: Wikipedia Orbital rendezvous for lower=faster and burn-speed=higher; Wikipedia Orbit phasing; derived numbers.)

misconceptions.belief: To catch the station you just fly toward it and speed up.
misconceptions.reality: Speeding up raises your orbit and slows your lap. You catch up by dropping lower, where you are faster, then raising back up.

misconceptions.belief: Crew-13 was the fastest trip to the station ever.
misconceptions.reality: NASA says fastest by a U.S. spacecraft. Russian Soyuz has done about 3 hours (Soyuz MS-17, Oct 2020).

misconceptions.belief: The ship flies at the station in a straight line, like a car chase.
misconceptions.reality: Both travel curved orbits at about 7.7 km/s; relative to each other they approach very slowly, a few cm/s at the end.

misconceptions.belief: Speed is limited by engine power; a stronger rocket would arrive sooner.
misconceptions.reality: The limit is geometry: where the station is on its lap at launch. NASA's Dragon program lead pointed to the station being in an opportune spot.

misconceptions.belief: Astronauts steer the docking by hand.
misconceptions.reality: Dragon docks autonomously with humans monitoring (Demo-2 crew did manual flying only up to about 220 m as a demonstration).

glossary.plain: A path where you keep falling around Earth without hitting it because you move sideways fast enough.
How long one lap around Earth takes (about 92-93 minutes for the station).
A short firing of the thrusters to change speed.
Using a different-length lap to change how far behind or ahead of the station you are.
The flat tilted sheet in space that the station's circle lies in.
A planned pause on approach where teams check everything before moving closer.
First a gentle link between ships, then latches that pull them tight and seal.

what_is_new_this_time: Verified: Crew-13 used a roughly 8-hour phasing profile (NASA: 'just under 8 hours in orbit phasing') and docked in 7 h 55 min, versus a previous US record of 12 h 33 min (uncrewed CRS-31, Nov 2024) and a Demo-2 trip of about 19 h. NASA's Dragon program lead attributed it largely to a favorable launch geometry (the station in an 'opportune spot'). UNVERIFIED: the exact count of orbits, number and timing of burns, and whether SpaceX changed the Dragon software or the profile versus earlier flights; no opened source says so.
open_questions: How many orbits and burns did Crew-13 use exactly (no opened source gives it)?

What are Dragon's real hold-point distances on approach?
What was Dragon's phasing orbit altitude?
NASA pre-launch said 7 h 50 min; actual 7 h 55 min. Which to say? Use the 7 h 55 min from NASA's post-docking blog.
